title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts regulatory activity and variant effects across cell states
generated_by: ChatGPT GPT-6; notes grounded in uploaded PDF
source_note: Sequential notes follow the article section order; info gives supporting detail and concl gives a takeaway when warranted. Methods notes follow main text.

items.q: What limitation does AlphaGenome 2 address?
items.a: Even strong DNA sequence-to-function models poorly distinguish related cell types or cell states and often need dataset-specific fine-tuning to predict regulatory activity and variant effects.

items.q: What is the key model change?
items.a: AlphaGenome 2 conditions a 1-Mb sequence model on tissue, cell type or cell state, training across bulk and single-cell datasets to predict condition-dependent regulatory activity.

items.q: What are the headline gains?
items.a: Compared with fine-tuned AG1 and specialized models, AG2 improves cell-state-specific gene expression, accessibility, eQTL effect prediction and enhancer–gene linking; it doubles recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision in a reported benchmark.
items.concl: Condition-aware learning materially improves the usefulness of genomic predictions for single-cell genetics.

items.q: Why do single-cell atlases not directly resolve most genetic variant effects?
items.a: Atlases typically cover many cell states but too few genotyped donors per state to map QTLs reliably. QTL fine-mapping also struggles with LD, low-frequency variants and limited tissue availability.

items.q: What can sequence-to-function models add to single-cell atlases?
items.a: Given a DNA sequence and cellular state, they can predict gene expression and chromatin phenotypes and compare reference and alternative alleles even where direct molecular QTL measurements are unavailable.

items.q: How does AG2 differ from the original AlphaGenome?
items.a: AG1 predicts a fixed inventory of bulk and cell-line tracks. AG2 combines early, throughout-network condition embeddings with single-cell training and an expression encoder to handle newly profiled cell states without fine-tuning.

items.q: What are the inputs and outputs?
items.a: Inputs are a 1-Mb human or mouse sequence, species, and a reference or expression-derived condition. Outputs include base/bin-level CAGE, RNA-seq, splicing, chromatin accessibility, histone/TF binding, CpG methylation, contact maps and gene expression.
items.info: Figure 1 depicts fixed condition embeddings and an optional single-cell expression encoder.

items.q: How is the biological condition incorporated?
items.a: Adaptive normalization uses a condition embedding to modulate representations in the encoder, transformer and decoder, not only an output-specific prediction head.
items.concl: Early conditioning lets the same DNA sequence produce distinct predictions for different cellular states.

items.q: What data were added relative to AG1?
items.a: AG2 adds 3,977 scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq pseudobulk tracks from 36 human/mouse studies, CpG methylation data for 185 human reference conditions, and post-training using 107 million human scRNA-seq profiles.
items.info: The expression encoder spans 68 tissues in the illustration accompanying Figure 1.

items.q: What are the four training phases?
items.a: Eight models undergo pretraining; condition embeddings and modulation layers are refined while the backbone is frozen; a single student distills average teacher predictions; post-training maps scRNA-derived expression representations into the frozen distilled model’s condition space.

items.q: What are reference and expression conditioning?
items.a: Reference conditioning selects a learned embedding for an ontology-defined tissue/cell type; expression conditioning infers that embedding from a measured scRNA-seq profile of a new condition.
items.concl: Expression conditioning extends AG2 to unseen cell states without retraining the sequence model.

items.q: What resources does the model generate?
items.a: The authors produce genome-wide enhancer–gene predictions across 640 conditions and scores for about 7 million common/trait-associated variants across 510 conditions.

items.q: How is tissue-specific gene-expression prediction assessed?
items.a: The authors compare predicted and observed per-gene log fold changes against tissue means, isolating tissue-specific differences from overall expression.

items.q: How much better is AG2 across GTEx tissues?
items.a: Median per-tissue Pearson r is 0.71 for AG2 versus 0.61 for AG1, and explained cross-tissue expression variance is 53% versus 41%.
items.concl: Conditioning improves representation of tissue-dependent expression patterns.

items.q: How well does AG2 represent differences among cell types?
items.a: Across human/mouse scRNA pseudobulks it explains a median 34% of within-tissue cell-type expression variance versus 23% for AG1-sc; for scATAC peaks the corresponding figures are 60% versus 51%.

items.q: What biological examples demonstrate finer specificity?
items.a: AG2 captures mouse tuft-cell-specific Trpm5 expression/accessibility and hematopoietic differentiation expression trajectories more faithfully than AG1-sc on held-out DNA.

items.q: Which architectural component drives the gain?
items.a: Matched-data ablations show that conditioning in the early encoder and transformer produces much of the benefit; restricting conditioning to output/decoder layers yields relatively little improvement.
items.concl: Both the larger corpus and where the condition acts inside the network matter.

items.section: Results – Improved prediction of non-coding variant effects
items.q: What QTL evaluation tasks are used?
items.a: Fine-mapped variants on held-out chromosomes are evaluated for causal-variant prioritization, direction of effect (sign), and effect magnitude (coefficient).

items.section: Results – Improved prediction of non-coding variant effects
items.q: How does AG2 perform on bulk-tissue GTEx eQTLs?
items.a: Across 49 tissues, causal eQTL recall at 90% precision rises from 17% (AG1) to 26% (AG2); sign recall at 90% accuracy rises from 32% to 40%.
items.info: Causality AUPRC 0.74 for AG2 versus 0.72 AG1 and 0.69 Borzoi; sign-area metric 0.85 versus 0.83 and 0.77.

items.section: Results – Improved prediction of non-coding variant effects
items.q: Where are the GTEx improvements most pronounced?
items.a: AG2’s gain over AG1 is driven primarily by eQTLs with putative tissue-specific effects. Other bulk QTL tasks such as splicing, accessibility, DNase and polyadenylation remain broadly comparable to AG1.

items.section: Results – Improved prediction of non-coding variant effects
items.q: How does AG2 score on TenK10K and IBDverse single-cell QTLs?
items.a: For TenK10K sc-eQTLs, recall at 90% precision improves from 16% (AG1-sc) to 30% (AG2), and sign recall at 90% accuracy from 23% to 43%. For intestinal IBDverse sc-eQTL sign, recall rises from 31% to 45%.
items.info: Benchmarks include 28 sc-eQTL cell types and 24 sc-caQTL cell types in TenK10K, and 47 non-blood cell types in IBDverse.

items.section: Results – Improved prediction of non-coding variant effects
items.q: Does predictive power decline with distance from the TSS?
items.a: Distance matters, but among eQTL variants overlapping accessible chromatin, predictions remain strong even beyond 35 kb from the TSS. Outside accessible peaks, all compared models perform substantially worse.
items.info: For TenK10K in accessible peaks beyond 35 kb, sign AUROC 0.86 AG2 versus 0.78 AG1-sc and effect-size Spearman ρ 0.57 versus 0.47.
items.concl: Accessibility context is important when interpreting distal variant scores.

items.section: Results – Improved prediction of non-coding variant effects
items.q: What happens when bulk PBMC training tracks are withheld?
items.a: An AG2 model trained without bulk PBMC tracks retains similar single-cell QTL performance in TenK10K; effect-size Spearman correlation decreases only modestly, from 0.47 to 0.45.
items.concl: The gains do not simply result from memorizing bulk blood tracks.

items.section: Results – Improved prediction of non-coding variant effects
items.q: What disease-related examples demonstrate cell-type-specific effects?
items.a: The paper illustrates variants affecting IL20RA and variants linked to congenital hyperinsulinism/HK1, where cell-state-resolved scores provide more specific mechanistic interpretation than aggregate tissue predictions.

items.q: What does cross-modality imputation mean here?
items.a: Because condition embeddings are separated from modality output heads, AG2 can predict an assay type for a cell condition even when that assay was not measured for that condition.

items.q: How is the ability to impute missing assays tested?
items.a: The authors withhold experimental tracks across assay types and conditions, then evaluate inferred signal in comparison with measured data and appropriate baselines.
items.info: The Results describe a held-out test of 184 bulk tracks across 30 conditions.

items.q: Why is imputation useful for scRNA-based analysis?
items.a: It permits prediction of accessibility and other epigenomic readouts in a cell population profiled by expression but not by matched ATAC- or ChIP-seq, enabling regulatory variant scoring in data-sparse states.
items.concl: Conditioning does not require every cell type to have every modality measured.

items.section: Results – Generalizing to new cell states
items.q: How does the expression encoder handle an unseen cell state?
items.a: A separately trained scRNA expression autoencoder encodes cells; a lightweight adapter maps its latent representation into AG2’s frozen condition space, after which the DNA model predicts tracks for the new condition.

items.section: Results – Generalizing to new cell states
items.q: What is frozen during the post-training phase?
items.a: The distilled genomic sequence model remains frozen while the mapping from expression-derived cell representations to conditioning vectors is trained.

items.section: Results – Generalizing to new cell states
items.q: Does expression conditioning outperform fine-tuning on target datasets?
items.a: Across related cell-type groups and unseen test cohorts, expression conditioning predicts condition-specific expression more accurately than dataset-specific fine-tuning in reported comparisons.
items.info: Reported paired tests include P = 3.1 × 10⁻¹² across 147 groups and P = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ across 20 unseen test groups.

items.section: Results – Generalizing to new cell states
items.q: What do Parkinson’s and vaccine-response cohort evaluations test?
items.a: They evaluate expression-conditioned predictions and variant effects in new single-cell cohorts or states, including Parkinson’s-related brain populations and vaccine-induced CD8+ T-cell states, rather than simply reusing a fixed condition label.

items.section: Results – Generalizing to new cell states
items.q: What is the advantage of using only a single-cell expression profile for conditioning?
items.a: A new dataset can generate cell-state-specific regulatory predictions without experimental sequencing of all other modalities or retraining the DNA sequence network.
items.concl: This makes the system more deployable to sparse or novel cell states.

items.section: Results – Predicting enhancer–gene links at scale
items.q: How are distal enhancer–gene links scored?
items.a: The model computes the gradient of predicted expression for a target gene with respect to a 1-Mb DNA sequence centered on the gene TSS; gradient magnitudes are aggregated over candidate regulatory elements.

items.section: Results – Predicting enhancer–gene links at scale
items.q: How does AG2 perform in a CRISPRi enhancer–gene benchmark?
items.a: On 4,378 element–gene pairs across five held-out cell lines, AG2 reaches AUPRC 0.78 versus AG1 0.73, Borzoi ensemble 0.61 and ENCODE-rE2G 0.57.
items.info: The paper reports a pronounced advantage in its distal element–gene distance bin (AG2 AUPRC 0.62 versus AG1 0.48, ENCODE-rE2G 0.37 and Borzoi 0.28).
items.concl: AG2’s relative strength increases for long-range enhancer–gene relationships.

items.section: Results – Predicting enhancer–gene links at scale
items.q: Does AG2 generalize to primary astrocytes?
items.a: On a CRISPRi screen in cultured primary human astrocytes, AG2 reports AUPRC 0.68 versus AG1 0.64 and Borzoi 0.49.

items.section: Results – Predicting enhancer–gene links at scale
items.q: What does the lineage-specific enhancer example illustrate?
items.a: The analysis uses a variant in a regulatory element affecting erythroid-lineage activity and shows that predicted regulatory effects differ from those in naive B cells, consistent with different cellular enhancer activity.

items.section: Results – Predicting enhancer–gene links at scale
items.q: What large-scale E2G resource was produced?
items.a: Predicted enhancer–gene links are supplied across 640 reference conditions, extending linked regulatory element annotations into numerous primary cell states.

items.section: Results – Interpreting complex-trait variants across cell types
items.q: Which three questions must a GWAS interpretation answer?
items.a: Which linked variant is functional, which gene it affects, and in which cell type or state the effect occurs.

items.section: Results – Interpreting complex-trait variants across cell types
items.q: What does the IBD 21q22 example show?
items.a: At an IBD-associated locus, AG2 prioritizes rs2836882 out of seven fine-mapped candidates, predicts an effect on ETS2 roughly 290 kb away rather than nearer genes, and localizes the effect to monocytes/macrophages.
items.info: The paper cites prior experimental chromatin and perturbation evidence supporting the mechanism.
items.concl: A condition-aware model can connect variant, distant target gene, and responsible cell lineage.

items.section: Results – Interpreting complex-trait variants across cell types
items.q: What variant atlas is scored?
items.a: Nearly seven million fine-mapped GWAS and common gnomAD variants (minor allele frequency >5%) across 510 reference conditions spanning human tissues and cell types.
items.info: These are precomputed candidate regulatory scores, not experimentally established causal labels.

items.section: Results – Interpreting complex-trait variants across cell types
items.q: Why score many cell types rather than a generic tissue?
items.a: A variant can alter a gene only within a narrow lineage, so aggregating signals across tissues may conceal relevant associations and the direction of the effect.

items.section: Results – Interpreting complex-trait variants across cell types
items.q: What can the atlas contribute to complex-trait interpretation?
items.a: It provides putative effects on genes and cellular states, enabling variant prioritization and hypotheses for GWAS loci including those without known eQTL colocalization.
items.concl: Computational variant maps can nominate targets for validation but do not replace association and perturbation data.

items.q: What general advance does the paper establish?
items.a: Combining early conditional sequence modeling with organism-scale single-cell atlases yields better cell-specific track and variant predictions, supports assay imputation, and generalizes to unseen scRNA-seq cell states.

items.q: What are the main remaining limitations?
items.a: High-precision recall still covers only a minority of fine-mapped eQTLs/GWAS candidate variants; effects are underestimated outside accessible chromatin, at some distal regions, or through post-transcriptional mechanisms. Transient, stimulated, disease and fine-grained neuronal states remain underrepresented.
items.concl: A predicted lack of effect is not strong evidence of biological neutrality.

items.q: Can condition embeddings infer outcomes of gene knockouts or dynamic state transitions?
items.a: Not reliably established. Because embeddings largely learn observational steady-state data, they describe correlations and the authors explicitly leave prediction of knockouts, overexpression and cell-state transitions unresolved.

items.q: What future directions do the authors propose?
items.a: Expand training modalities and cell types, including footprinting, brain atlases and perturbation datasets; add species; and adapt spatial or other inputs into the same condition space.
items.info: The paper mentions lightweight adapters and more efficient attribution as possible scaling directions.

items.q: How is a discrete condition encoded?
items.a: Ontology-defined reference conditions index learned embeddings that control adaptive normalization throughout the DNA sequence network.

items.q: How do single-cell data enter pretraining and post-training?
items.a: Pseudobulk scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq tracks provide reference condition targets; a separate large scRNA expression corpus trains a cell representation subsequently mapped to the frozen sequence model.

items.q: What is the distinction between student distillation and expression post-training?
items.a: Distillation trains one student to approximate an ensemble of sequence-model teachers on perturbed DNA. Post-training holds that student fixed and learns how expression-derived cell states condition its predictions.

items.q: How are generalization and benchmarking protected?
items.a: The authors use held-out genome intervals, held-out tracks or held-out single-cell datasets depending on the specific test, and compare with both fine-tuned AG1 and specialized methods.

items.q: How are variant effects and E2G links obtained?
items.a: Allelic effects compare reference- and alternate-sequence predictions for target conditions; E2G uses gene-expression attribution aggregated over candidate elements around each gene.

items.q: How should users interpret high or low regulatory variant scores?
items.a: A high score is a model-based hypothesis of a context-specific effect; a low score does not exclude activity, especially in missing biological contexts or at mechanisms poorly captured by the training assays.
